questions.question: How does Sidekiq handle job retries and failures?
questions.title: Job Retry and Failure
questions.direct_answer: Sidekiq retries failed jobs automatically. By default a job retries 25 times with exponential backoff (15s, 30s, 60s, ... up to ~21 days), then moves to the dead set (morgue). You configure: `sidekiq_options retry: 5` (5 retries) or `retry: 0` (no retries) or `retry: 600`. The job's perform is wrapped in your sidekiq_retries_exhausted block for final handling. Failures are usually network/timeout blips, so retrying with backoff often self-heals. Dead jobs are viewable in the Sidekiq Web UI (/sidekiq/retries, /sidekiq/morgue) and can be retried manually. To make a job idempotent (safe to retry), ensure performing it twice has the same effect as once (check before create; use unique job ids). Don't retry non-retryable errors (a bad arg) — rescue them and re-raise with a 'skip' class, or set retry: 0 for that job.

sections.content:
retries with backoff (default 25x) then dead set. sidekiq_options retry: N. Idempotent jobs. Web UI.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  J[job fails] --> R[retry: 25 (default)]
  R --> B[backoff: 15s 30s 60s...]
  R -->|exhausted| D[dead set / morgue]
```

sections.title: Sidekiq retry and failure
sections.content:
```ruby
class MailJob
  include Sidekiq::Job
  sidekiq_options retry: 5          # 5 retries (default 25, exp backoff)
  # sidekiq_options retry: 0        # no retries (fail fast)
  # sidekiq_options retry: 600      # lots of retries

  def perform(user_id)
    user = User.find(user_id)
    Mailer.welcome(user).deliver_now
  end
end

# Default backoff: 15s, 30s, 60s, 2m, 4m, 8m, ... up to ~21 days, 25 tries.
# Failures (network/timeout blips) often self-heal on retry.

# Final handling when retries are exhausted:
class MailJob
  sidekiq_retries_exhausted do |msg, ex|
    logger.error "giving up on #{msg}: #{ex.message}"
    # alert, enqueue a cleanup job, etc.
  end
end

# After retries exhausted -> DEAD SET (morgue):
#   Sidekiq Web UI:  /sidekiq/retries  (in-flight retries)
#                   /sidekiq/morgue   (dead jobs; retry manually)

# Make jobs IDEMPOTENT (safe to retry): running twice == once.
  # - check before create (don't duplicate)
  # - use unique job ids / dedupe
  # - money: use a payment idempotency key

# Non-retryable errors (bad arg): don't retry forever.
  # rescue SpecificError => e; raise  # OR  sidekiq_options retry: 0
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Retrying non-idempotent jobs (double charges/emails — make them idempotent).
Retrying non-retryable errors (bad arg) forever — use retry: 0 or skip.
Forgetting idempotency keys for money (double charges on retry).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Sidekiq retries failed jobs automatically (default 25x, exponential backoff).
Configure: sidekiq_options retry: 5 (or retry: 0 for no retries).
After retries are exhausted, the job moves to the dead set (morgue).
View/retry via the Sidekiq Web UI: /sidekiq/retries, /sidekiq/morgue.
Make jobs idempotent (running twice == once) so retries are safe; use idempotency keys.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Sidekiq retries failed jobs automatically. By default a job retries 25 times with exponential backoff (15s, 30s, 60s, dot dot dot up to about 21 days), then moves to the dead set (morgue). You configure: sidekiq options retry 5 (5 retries) or retry 0 (no retries) or retry 600. The job's perform is wrapped in your sidekiq retries exhausted block for final handling. Failures are usually network or timeout blips, so retrying with backoff often self-heals. Dead jobs are viewable in the Sidekiq Web UI (slash sidekiq retries, slash sidekiq morgue) and can be retried manually. To make a job idempotent (safe to retry), ensure performing it twice has the same effect as once (check before create; use unique job ids). Don't retry non-retryable errors (a bad arg) — rescue them and re-raise with a skip class, or set retry 0 for that job. A common mistake is retrying non-idempotent jobs, like double charges, when you should make them idempotent.
